t: LeetCode 1541 — Minimum Insertions to Balance a Parentheses String
o: Unusually, each "(" must be closed by TWO consecutive right parentheses "))". Scanning left to right with a pool of unmatched "(" handles everything greedily: on seeing ")" we first complete the pair — consuming the next ")" if present, otherwise paying one insertion — then match the completed "))" against an open "(" from the pool, paying another insertion if the pool is empty. Example 1 "(()))" shows the stray final ")" costing exactly one insertion; example 3 "))())(" costs three: one "(" inserted for the leading pair and both characters of a trailing "))" inserted for the leftover "(". Whatever opens remain at the end each need two insertions, and local greedy choices are globally optimal because insertions may go anywhere.
k: Treat "))" as one closing token; a lone ")" always costs exactly one inserted ")".
A completed close token with no available "(" costs one more insertion; every unmatched "(" left at the end costs two.
Greedy matching is optimal since insertions can be placed at any position.

a.i: Push every "(" onto a stack; when a close token arrives, pop if possible and otherwise charge one insertion for the missing "(". Leftover opens cost two insertions each. The stack makes the pairing mechanics explicit and easy to reason about.
s: Walk index i over s; push on "(".
On ")": consume the following ")" when present, else add 1 to res for the missing half.
Pop an open for this token; if the stack is empty add 1 to res.
After the scan add 2 per remaining open and return res.
a.t: O(n) — each character is examined once.
a.sp: O(n) — the stack can hold all opens.

a.i: The stack only ever stores identical "(" entries, so a plain integer open counter replaces it with identical logic and O(1) memory — the natural refinement once the pairing argument is clear.
s: On ")": consume the next ")" if present else res += 1; then decrement open or set res += 1 if none.
a.sp: O(1) — two counters and an index.

w: Call out the double-")" twist up front — most candidates pattern-match the classic one-to-one problem (LeetCode 921) and fail. Pitfalls: runs of ")" like ")))" where the middle paren pairs with neither neighbor cleanly, forgetting the final 2 * open term, and charging two insertions for a lone ")" instead of one plus a potential "(". Edge cases: a single "(" (answer 2), all closes, deeply nested strings. Follow-ups: reconstruct one minimal balanced string, or handle k consecutive closers per opener in general.
